Pierre du Moulin
pyair dū moo-lan'
n. (Pierre du Moulin, 1568–1658, pastor at Charenton, professor at Sedan, and champion of Dort against Arminius and Amyraut)
Greek Petros, a rock; French du Moulin, of the mill.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pierre du Moulin survived the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre as a child, studied at Cambridge and Leiden, and taught philosophy at Leiden, where Hugo Grotius was among his pupils. From 1599 to 1620 he was pastor of the Reformed church of Paris at Charenton and the most formidable Protestant controversialist in France, writing against the Jesuits, against the papal claims, and against the doctrine of the mass; his Buckler of the Faith of 1618 answered the king's Jesuit confessor point by point. He was equally firm against the Remonstrants. His Anatomy of Arminianism (1619) was one of the most widely read Reformed treatments of the controversy decided at Dort, and he led the French national synod of Alais in 1620 to adopt the Canons of Dort. Driven from Paris by royal displeasure in 1620, he spent the rest of his long life as professor of theology at the Protestant academy of Sedan, and from there he attacked Amyraut's hypothetical universalism as a revival of Arminianism under Reformed terms. James I of England valued him and gave him a prebend at Canterbury. His theology was that of Dort, resting on the sovereignty of grace: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a controversialist as one who carries on a controversy, and Arminianism as the doctrines of the Arminians.

CONTROVER'SIALIST, n. One who carries on a controversy; a disputant.

ARMIN'IANISM, n. The peculiar doctrines or tenets of the Arminians.

BUCK'LER, n. A kind of shield, or piece of defensive armor.

Modern Corruption

The French champion of Dort who answered Rome, Arminius, and Amyraut in turn.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Du Moulin's career shows why the Reformed churches of France adopted Dort: they had learned that a doctrine of grace that leaves the decisive act to the human will is a doctrine Rome can accept. His answer to the Remonstrants was Paul's, “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).

The principle to recover is the readiness he showed on every front, “to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15). The French church that later gave Amyraut a hearing and silence instead of an answer did not find the peace it sought.

Usage

"“it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — the Anatomy of Arminianism in brief."

"“not of him that willeth” (Rom 9:16) — his answer to the Remonstrants."

"“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jude 1:3) — sixty years of controversy."
